content.p: On the morning of Palm Sunday, 27 March 1836, Mexican soldiers marched hundreds of captured Texan volunteers out of the old Spanish presidio at Goliad, turned on them at close range and shot them. The prisoners had surrendered a week earlier believing they would be treated as prisoners of war and sent home. The Handbook of Texas, the standard reference of the Texas State Historical Association, calls the killing the most infamous episode of the Texas Revolution. A man-by-man study of the command, it says, shows that 342 were executed that day, 28 escaped the firing lines, and about 20 more were spared.

The order came from Antonio López de Santa Anna, president of Mexico and commander of its army in Texas. The general who took the surrender, José de Urrea, had asked for leniency. The colonel left in charge at Goliad, José Nicolás de la Portilla, had two conflicting orders in his hands and chose the harsher one. Within weeks the victims' fate had become a rallying cry for the army that defeated Santa Anna at San Jacinto.

The killings had a legal pretext in Mexico's own law. According to the Handbook, Santa Anna had watched how New Orleans reacted when 28 men captured in an expedition against Tampico were tried as pirates and shot on 14 December 1835. Concluding that the reaction was mild, he obtained from the Mexican Congress a decree of 30 December 1835 directing that foreigners taken in arms against the government be treated as pirates and shot. The Handbook's authors describe Santa Anna as acting "within Mexican law", while stressing that the massacre cannot be understood apart from this earlier legislation.

Carrying out the decree on the Texas coast fell to Urrea, who commanded Santa Anna's right wing. The Handbook, quoting Urrea's contemporary Reuben Potter, says he was disposed to treat prisoners with leniency when he was not overruled by a superior. After the fight at San Patricio on 27 February 1836 and the battle of Agua Dulce Creek, Urrea first issued an order to shoot his prisoners, but after a priest, Father Thomas J. Malloy, protested, he sent them to Matamoros and asked Santa Anna's pardon. At Refugio on 15 March he was less restrained: the Handbook says he had Captain Amon B. King and fourteen of his men shot, while freeing the colonists and Mexicans among the captives. King's company had earlier angered local people by burning ranchos and shooting eight Mexicans seated around a campfire, the Handbook adds.

Fannin, born about 1804 in Georgia, had left West Point after about two years and moved to Texas in 1834. The Handbook says his own letters show he was a slave trader. He took part in the early fighting of the revolution and was commissioned a colonel in the regular army in December 1835. By February 1836 he was at Goliad, where the old presidio of La Bahía, taken by Texans in October 1835, had been renamed Fort Defiance.

He was not an easy man to follow. One of his men, J. G. Ferguson, wrote to his brother that most of the soldiers disliked him because he seemed to want greatness without taking the proper steps toward it. Fannin, for his part, wrote in February that he did not want command and felt incompetent. When William Barret Travis begged him for help at the Alamo, Fannin set out with about 320 men and four cannons on 26 February, according to HistoryNet, and turned back after a very short distance, judging the column insufficiently supplied. The Alamo fell on 6 March.

Sam Houston then ordered Fannin to fall back to Victoria. The Handbook says Fannin delayed because the detachments of King and William Ward were still out near Refugio; only when he heard that they had been captured did he begin his retreat, on 19 March. Urrea's army caught his column on open ground near Coleto Creek.

After a day of fighting in a defensive square, the Texans, short of water and ammunition, asked for terms. The Handbook says Fannin's men wanted to be treated as prisoners of war and paroled and returned to the United States as soon as possible. Urrea could not accept that in light of Santa Anna's orders, but the Texans still had their rifles, spare muskets and nine brass cannons and could have made a costly fight of it. He therefore proposed his own written terms: the Texans would lay down their arms and become prisoners "at the disposal of the Supreme Mexican Government". Urrea assured Fannin he knew of no prisoner who had trusted Mexican clemency and lost his life, and said he would recommend acceptance and expected an answer from Santa Anna within eight days.

Fannin accepted, the Handbook says, without telling his men that the terms were conditional. One of the Mexican commissioners, Major Juan José Holsinger, put them at ease with the words "Well, gentlemen! In eight days, home and liberty!" The blog Still Current makes the same point: Fannin agreed to an unconditional surrender but did not tell his officers and men.

Roughly 230 or 240 unhurt or lightly wounded men were marched back to Goliad and held in the presidio's chapel. About fifty wounded, Fannin among them, followed over the next two days, and on 25 March some eighty men of Ward's Georgia Battalion, captured near Dimitt's Landing, joined them. Urrea wrote to Santa Anna recommending clemency, but, the Handbook notes, he said nothing of the terms the Texans themselves had drafted.

Santa Anna answered on 23 March, according to the Handbook, ordering the immediate execution of the "perfidious foreigners" and repeating the order the next day. The same day, apparently doubting that Urrea would do it, he sent a direct order to the officer commanding Goliad. Portilla received it on 26 March. Two hours later, the Handbook says, came a message from Urrea telling him to treat the prisoners with consideration, Fannin especially, and to put them to work rebuilding the town. The Handbook suggests Urrea knew Portilla could not comply: on 25 March he had ordered reinforcements out of the garrison, leaving too few guards for such a work gang. World History Encyclopedia dates Santa Anna's letter to 26 March rather than 23 March, so the sources differ on the date of the order.

Portilla, in the Handbook's words, spent an unquiet night, then concluded he had to obey Santa Anna and ordered the prisoners shot at dawn. On the evening of 26 March, the prisoners had been in good spirits. Fannin had come back that day from Copano, where he and his adjutant, Joseph Chadwick, had accompanied Mexican officers in an effort to charter a vessel; the Handbook says the real aim was to commandeer the ship, which had already left. He told his men that the Mexicans were making arrangements for their departure, and that night they sang "Home Sweet Home".

At sunrise the unwounded prisoners were roused and formed into three groups under heavy guard, the Handbook says. They were given different explanations: that they would gather wood, drive cattle, march to Matamoros or go to Copano for passage to New Orleans. The largest group, including Ward's Georgia men, went along the Béxar road. Others, among them the San Antonio Grays and the Mobile Grays, took the Victoria road, and Captain John Shackelford's Red Rovers and Ira Westover's regulars took the San Patricio road.

Between half a mile and three-quarters of a mile from the presidio each column was halted. The guards on one side countermarched to join those on the other, and at a signal they fired at a range too close to miss. Nearly all were killed in the first volley, and those who were not were pursued and killed with gunfire, bayonet or lance. From the two groups on the river roads, twenty-four men reached the woods along the stream. From the San Patricio road, where there was less cover, only four are known to have got away.

Back at the presidio the wounded were killed. The Handbook says Fannin and some forty wounded men (the Mexican officer José Enrique de la Peña estimated eighty or ninety) were put to death within the presidio under Captain Carolino Huerta. HistoryNet, drawing on an account by a Texan spared for his language skills, says Fannin was among the last to die. He gave the officer of the firing squad his money and gold watch in return for a promise that the watch would go to his family, that he would be shot in the heart rather than the face and that he would be buried as a Christian. According to that account the officer took the watch anyway and had Fannin shot through the face.

No source gives a single agreed number. The Handbook reports that Portilla wrote that he held 445 prisoners, not counting the roughly eighty men of William P. Miller's Nashville Battalion, who had been captured without arms at Copano and were to be spared. Texan sources, it says, put the figure at 407. It adds that some of those taken at Refugio were kept alive because they worked for the Mexican army as blacksmiths and wheelwrights, and that the fate of others is unknown. World History Encyclopedia says only that 350 to 400 were executed, and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department speaks of about 350 men held at the presidio. The 342 figure comes from the muster-based study cited in the Handbook, which subtracts those who escaped or were spared.

Some survivors had narrow escapes. William Lockhart Hunter, a sergeant, was not killed by the volleys and, by one account, lay still until bayoneted in the shoulder and cut at the throat; the Handbook entry on him records another version in which Nicholas Fagan, a spared blacksmith, found him and carried him to a Mexican family. Isaac D. Hamilton, one of four Red Rovers to survive, was recaptured, sent to Victoria and slated to be shot again until news of San Jacinto produced confusion in the Mexican camp and let him escape once more, with help from Francisca de Alavez. Dillard Cooper, only slightly wounded at Coleto, also escaped, and an account by him appeared in the Columbus Citizen in 1870.

Others were not at Goliad at all. Albert Clinton Horton, who led a scouting patrol at Coleto Creek, turned back to find the army surrounded and fled with his men on 19 March, an act the Handbook says saved his life but dogged his political career.

The Handbook credits the entreaties of a woman the Texans called the "Angel of Goliad", Francita Alavez, together with the kindly intervention of Colonel Francisco Garay, for the sparing of about twenty men as doctors, orderlies, interpreters or mechanics. World History Encyclopedia says she was the wife of Captain Telesforo Alavez and suggested that some be spared, and that she hid others before the killing. The Handbook says Urrea held about twenty of Ward's men to build boats at Victoria and that she persuaded her husband, in charge there, to spare them too; they later escaped. Two doctors, Joseph Barnard and John Shackelford, were instead sent to San Antonio to tend Mexican soldiers wounded in the Alamo assault; both got away later.

The reprieve of Miller's men did not last. About a week after Goliad, the Handbook says, Santa Anna ordered them and the other spared men shot, then cancelled the order the next day. They were marched to Matamoros after San Jacinto, and most stayed there until Mexico released them.

The Handbook argues that until Goliad Santa Anna had a reputation for cunning rather than cruelty. At that point Texas had no other army in the field, and its provisional government seemed unable to raise one. It reasons that had the prisoners instead been shipped home to New Orleans, Texas's standing in the United States might have fallen. Instead, it says, the volleys at Goliad and the fall of the Alamo branded Santa Anna and the Mexican people as cruel and stirred anger in Texas, the United States and even Britain and France.

World History Encyclopedia says the Alamo and Goliad together set off the Runaway Scrape, the mass flight of settlers eastward, and that Houston's army swelled with volunteers eager to avenge the dead. At San Jacinto on 21 April 1836 they attacked, according to HistoryNet, shouting "Remember the Alamo! Goliad! Labadie!" (an Anglo mispronunciation of La Bahía). The battle lasted about eighteen minutes, World History Encyclopedia says, and Santa Anna was captured. HistoryNet observes that Goliad lacked the Alamo's fame partly because the Alamo's defenders died fighting while the Goliad men were executed.
content.h2: The unmarked grave and the monument
content.p: After the killing the bodies were burned and left to weather and scavengers until 3 June 1836, when General Thomas J. Rusk, passing through Goliad in pursuit of the retreating Mexican army, gathered the remains and buried them with military honors; some survivors were present. The grave stayed unmarked. About 1858 a Goliad merchant, George von Dohlen, piled rocks on what was believed to be the spot. In April 1885 a memorial was put up in the town, not at the grave, by a Fannin Monument Association formed by the survivor William L. Hunter.

In 1930 Goliad Boy Scouts found charred bone fragments that animals had unearthed. A New Year's Day excursion in 1932 drew in University of Texas anthropologist J. E. Pearce, and historians Clarence R. Wharton and Harbert Davenport confirmed the site. Money was appropriated in 1936, the Texas Centennial year, for a large pink granite monument, which was dedicated on 4 June 1938. Davenport gave the address, later published as "The Men of Goliad".

The monument stands just east of Presidio La Bahía, which the Texas Historical Commission now operates, and marks the common burial site of Fannin and his men. Between the presidio and the monument is a statue of Francisca Alvarez, dedicated in March 2004 by her descendants. The Fannin Battleground State Historic Site, about nine miles east of Goliad, marks the place where Fannin's column was captured.
